activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
story:
Harrison stood at the counter with an onion, a cutting board, and a very sharp knife that Ms. Katz had just handed him. "Claw grip," she said, curling her own fingers so the knuckles stuck out like a small wall. "Tuck the fingertips away, and let the knife ride against the knuckles." Harrison copied her, feeling clumsy, and made his first slow slice. The onion layers came apart in pale rings, and his eyes began to sting.

"I read that chilling the onion first helps," said Abrielle, who was measuring out canned tomatoes at the stove. "There's a whole controversy online about whether that's true or just something people repeat."

"Everything about onions has a controversy," said Simon, grating cheese with more enthusiasm than skill. Harrison smiled behind his clawed hand and kept cutting, allocating his attention between the onion and the empty pot waiting beside him. He had wanted to make the sauce from scratch because his mom worked late on Thursdays, and tonight he wanted dinner to be his job, not hers.

He got bolder. The slices turned into a rough dice, faster now, and he was reaching for the salt when his elbow knocked the knife. It slid off the counter, handle first, blade spinning down toward the floor. His hand shot out on its own, reaching, and then he caught himself. He stepped back instead and let it fall. The knife hit the linoleum with a loud clatter and lay there, blade flat, harmlessly gleaming.

"You didn't grab it," Abrielle said, staring at him. "My cousin grabbed one at our campsite last summer. Trying to catch a falling knife is how everybody gets cut, the nurse told him."

"I don't know why I stopped," Harrison said. His heart was still thumping, but the kitchen felt quiet again, the sauce bubbling softly behind them. He crouched down, picked the knife up carefully by the handle, and washed it under the tap before setting it back on the board, well away from the edge this time.

Ms. Katz glanced over from the stove, said nothing, and slid the diced onion into the hot oil. It hissed and filled the kitchen with a sweet smell. Harrison positioned the knife flat on the counter, then nudged it a few inches further in, until he was sure. "Okay," he said, picking up the wooden spoon. "Now somebody teach me how to tell when the garlic's done."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: An external stylesheet is connected to a web page by a link tag with rel="stylesheet" placed inside the page's head section.
story:
Xavier hit refresh for the fourth time and his heading stayed stuck in the top left corner of the screen like a bird refusing to fly. The tech cabin smelled of hot laptops and bug spray, and outside the window the lake glittered, but he barely noticed. His whole plan, a web page for the camp's Friday showcase with a giant centred title reading CAMP ECHO LAKE 2025, was not cooperating. He had typed the styles into a file called style.css exactly the way the sheet Mr. Morales had handed out showed. Heading selector, curly braces, the works. Nothing happened.

"It worked for me," said Samson, leaning over from the next seat. "Mine's centred and everything." Samson spun his laptop around as proof, and Xavier felt a hot flicker of jealousy, then something sharper: curiosity. Two files, the same lesson, different results. That meant something invisible was going on. There was a rule hiding somewhere, and Xavier wanted to find it before the suspense of a broken page ruined his week.

He remembered Tuesday, the first day of camp, when Mabel's flashlight had gone dark on the night hike and everyone panicked until she found the switch was half clicked, not off, not on. The battery was fine. The connection was the problem. Xavier sat up straight. Maybe his page had a connection problem too. The styles lived in a separate file, style.css, so the page had to be told about it somehow. He scrolled to the top of his HTML and stared at the head section, where his title tag sat all alone. On Samson's screen, one line sat there that his did not. Samson had a link tag with rel="stylesheet" pointing at style.css, placed inside the head.

"That's it," Xavier said. "The stylesheet is external, so the page needs a link tag in the head to reach it." He typed the line in, letter by letter, his fingers buzzing. Refresh. The heading floated gently to the exact centre of the page, and Xavier actually yelped. Mabel slid her chair over so fast it squeaked on the floorboards.

"Show me," she demanded. "My buttons look like dead grey bricks." Xavier paraphrased what he'd found in one sentence, checked her file, and pointed at the same missing line. She added it, hit refresh, and her buttons bloomed into bright blue.

Mr. Morales wandered past and whistled at Xavier's screen. "Nice work. You know, good design is subjective, but centred? Centred is just right." Xavier grinned and dragged his chair between Samson and Mabel, the three laptops glowing together in the dim cabin like a tiny city at night. "Now," he said, cracking his knuckles, "let's make the background dark."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
story:
Sophie had claimed the best spot on the bleachers hours before the puck dropped, because the community sports field's big screen was the only place in the neighbourhood showing the final game, and she was not about to squint at it from behind the snack shack. Cheikh sat on her left, holding nachos like they were treasure. Charles-Etienne sat on her right, wearing a jersey two sizes too big because he insisted it was lucky, even though it had never once been lucky.

Between periods, the screen showed a slow pan over the trophy, and Cheikh frowned. "Why does it look so beat up? It's got dents and scratches and names all over it. Are they too poor to buy a new one?"

"They're not poor," Charles-Etienne said, defiant, as though the trophy's honour were his own. "Players make fortunes. That's their whole income, playing. They could buy a hundred shiny cups."

Sophie studied the screen while the crowd around them argued about the referee's last call. The dents formed a pattern, she thought. Every team that won had left marks, and nobody had polished them away. That meant the trophy wasn't old because nobody cared. It was old on purpose. She remembered a museum trip and a plaque she had read half a dozen times, and something clicked into place.

"It's not that they can't afford a new one," she said. "It's the oldest trophy in North American professional sports. Lord Stanley, who was Canada's governor general, donated it in 1892, and it was first awarded in 1893. They keep it because of that."

Cheikh tested her immediately, because that was what Cheikh did. "Okay, then, who was Lord Stanley?"

"Canada's governor general," Sophie said. "It's called the Stanley Cup because of him."

"That's the only fact I know now," Cheikh admitted, "and I will recount it to everyone at school as if I always knew it."

Down on the field, Mr. Ahmadi, who coached the under-twelves and had wandered over from drills, overheard them and gave Sophie a thumbs up without slowing his walk. Charles-Etienne, however, was not ready to surrender. "A trophy from 1893 can't be the oldest. What about that giant silver football my uncle has? That's from 1890, I'm almost sure."

Sophie crossed her arms. "Professional sports. In North America. Is your uncle's football a professional trophy?"

Charles-Etienne opened his mouth, closed it, and then laughed so hard his lucky jersey rode up over his belly. "It's a bowling trophy from 1994 and it says so on the bottom. Fine. You win. But if the game goes to overtime, I'm still blaming the jersey, not you."

The horn sounded for the third period, and the crowd rose in one wave. Cheikh raised his nachos above his head like a torch, and Sophie grabbed Charles-Etienne's sleeve and pulled them both up to stand. "Watch the screen," she said. "History's either getting a dent tonight or getting a new set of names."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
story:
Samantha stood at the hotel room window, looking down at the harbor where the ferry sat tied to its dock. Tomorrow's crossing to the island would take ninety minutes, and if Axl got sick again, her mother had said they might eliminate the ferry entirely and drive the long way around, which would cost them the whale watch. Her motive for fixing this was simple: she was not missing those whales.

"You look like a ghost," she told Axl, who lay on the far bed with a wristband pressed to his forehead. He had spent the whole trip down reading in the car, and then tonight, on the little shuttle boat across the bay, he had turned green before they were halfway there. Samantha, meanwhile, had watched the shoreline slide past the whole time and felt fine.

"I get sick, you don't," Axl groaned. "That's the pattern."

"Maybe not." Samantha pulled out her notebook and drew two stick figures. One had eyes on a book, with wobbly lines for the stomach. The other had eyes on the far shore. "When the boat moved, my eyes were watching something far away and still, and my stomach stayed calm. Your eyes were on a page, and everything felt wrong." She knew she might be biased in favor of her own theory, since she was the one who felt fine, but there was a way to check it. "Come to the window. Look at the horizon, that line where the water meets the sky. Don't look at anything close."

Axl dragged himself over. For a minute nothing happened, and Samantha began to worry she had made it worse. Then his shoulders dropped, and he let out a long breath. "Huh," he said. "The swimming feeling is going away. Keep talking, I'm not looking away."

The next morning on the ferry, Samantha was so sure of herself that she sat inside at a table and played cards with Emy-Jade the entire crossing, cards flying, heads down, laughing at Emy-Jade's terrible cheat of hiding jokers under her sleeve. By the time the island came into view, Samantha's stomach was rolling like the sea itself. Emy-Jade, who had also been staring at cards, felt perfectly fine.

Axl appeared in the doorway with the smuggest face she had ever seen. He held out his hand. "Come on," he said. "The deck's this way, and the horizon isn't going anywhere."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
Gabrielle pressed her palm flat against the page of the Quran as if she could push the words into her hand. Surah Al-Mulk had thirty verses, and she had to recite it from memory at the ceremony in three weeks. In the quiet corner of the mosque after Sunday class, she whispered the eighth verse, stumbled, and started over.

"You skipped a line," said Katia, sitting cross-legged beside her with her own copy open. Katia was only reciting ten verses for the same ceremony, and she already had them perfect.

"I didn't skip it. It evaporated." Gabrielle stared at the page. "My brain is broken."

"Your brain is fine. Ms. Gupta says remembering is like a path through grass. Walk it enough times and it stays."

Gabrielle did not answer. She was watching the young man across the prayer hall, an older cousin of a girl in her class, standing near the bookshelf with his eyes closed. His lips were moving. He was reciting something long, and he was not holding a book, because there was no book in his hands at all.

She got up and walked over. "Excuse me. How are you doing that without looking?"

He opened his eyes and smiled. "I'm a hafiz. That's what they call someone who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters."

"All of it? In your head?"

"All of it. It doesn't stay there by itself, though. I have to practice constantly, every single day, or pieces slip."

Gabrielle thought about that all the way back to her corner. A whole book, kept alive only by daily walking of the path. She had imagined that once she memorized Surah Al-Mulk, she would be finished, and she could resign herself to never looking at the page again. That was wrong. Her cousin-in-recitation had not finished either. Nobody finished.

She turned back to verse eight, the one that kept vanishing. Instead of reading it ten times in a row, she tried something different. She recited it, then covered the page, then recited it again an hour later, after practicing verse nine, so her mind had to pull it up from farther away. Like a neuron firing down a path she had to keep clear, she thought. When she got it right twice in a row, she wrote a small symmetrical pair of checkmarks in the margin of her notebook, one for each success.

"Katia," she said. "Quiz me tomorrow before class. And the day after that."

"Every day?"

"Every day. Even after the ceremony."

Katia grinned and held out her hand. Gabrielle shook it, then closed her notebook, tucked the Quran under her arm, and headed for the shoe rack by the door.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Dylan had one job at the mall: find a birthday present for his mom before Pedro's hockey practice at four. He and Anaeve were cutting through the electronics store when he spotted the display laptops, all awake and lined up, and remembered the thing Mr. Leung had said back in September, something about search engines. He typed his own name into the search bar just to see.

The third result made his stomach drop. A comment on a restaurant review site, four years old, from "DylanRocks09," his whole name signed underneath: "Best pizza in town, we go every Friday after my games at Riverside Arena!" There was a photo of him at nine, holding a slice, grinning a gap-toothed grin. He'd forgotten the account completely. But there it was, public, findable by anyone who typed his name.

"That's you," Anaeve said, leaning in. "Why does it still exist? You deleted that app ages ago."

"That's the thing," Dylan said. "Deleting the app isn't deleting the post. The post was on the web, public." He scrolled down and found the answer in a help page: search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results. The copy wasn't on his phone. It lived somewhere he couldn't reach in and grab it, like a page torn out and filed in a drawer across town.

He tested it. In the mall's food court, he made Pedro type Dylan's name into Pedro's phone, on a different network, while Anaeve used the store laptop again. Both results appeared in seconds, identical. Pedro whistled. "So the Friday pizza, the arena, your face. Anyone could find that."

"Anyone," Dylan said. He opened the old site, logged in with a password he hadn't used since fifth grade, and deleted the comment and the photo, one tap after another. Then he checked the account settings and found three other old reviews, each one cheerful and public and full of exactly where he'd been. He deleted those too, though he knew the copies might already be indexed somewhere. At least he could stop adding.

By the time he'd finished, he had twenty minutes to buy his mom's present, and he chose the simple scarf instead of the extravagant perfume set he'd been eyeing. "My mom's the type who searches people," Anaeve said as they walked to the register. "She searched my math tutor once and found his old band photos."

Dylan paid, took the bag, and on the way out he glanced back at the display laptops, rows of them glowing with the search bars still open. "Next time," he said, "I'm typing in a fake name first."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
story:
Zack spotted Taha coming down Maple Street with his bike helmet dangling from one hand, and his stomach did a fast flip, because they hadn't spoken in nine days. Nine days since Taha had walked into the pizza place, seen Zack sharing a booth with Natalia and her project board, and turned straight around. Zack had chased him half a block, but Taha had only said, "Forget it," and pedaled off toward the affluent side of the neighborhood where his cousin lived, the part with the stone gates.

Zack planted himself in the middle of the sidewalk. "Taha. Wait."

Taha stopped, but he didn't look up. He was spinning the helmet strap around one finger, faster and faster, which was what he did when he was mad but didn't want to be. Down the block, Natalia was sitting on Ms. Khoury's front steps with a stack of cue cards, quizzing herself for the health test, and Zack had a wild, sudden idea.

"Taha, before you say anything," Zack said, "just listen to me try something." He jogged over to Natalia, grabbed one of her cards, and jogged back. "Okay. Active listening. That's this thing psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson came up with in 1957. It means you try to understand the speaker's point of view, and you prove it by repeating their meaning back in your own words. That's the whole card. That's the trick."

"Is this a joke to you?" Taha said.

"No. Watch." Zack took a breath. "You showed up at Sal's and I was sitting with Natalia instead of saving our usual seats, and you felt like I picked her over you."

Taha's finger stopped spinning. His shoulders came down about an inch. "You were supposed to help me integrate the new kid into our dodgeball team that same night. I texted you twice."

"So you felt like she came first and I blew you off."

"Yeah." Taha finally looked at him. "That's exactly it."

Zack held up the card like it was a winning lottery ticket. "See? It worked! It's literally a seventy-year-old trick and it worked!"

Natalia yelled from the steps, "That's Rogers and Farson, thank you very much, and if you're using my card you owe me a slice."

"Two slices," Zack called back, grinning. He turned to Taha. "Also, I was at Sal's because Natalia was helping me make a get-well poster for you. You were out all week with that antibiotic for your ear, and I couldn't exactly deliver it through your window."

Taha stared at him. "You made me a poster?"

"It's in my backpack. It has a drawing of your ear wearing a superhero cape."

Taha laughed, the loud snorting one, and slung his arm around Zack's neck. "Show me right now, and then slices, and then dodgeball. New kid's actually pretty good."

Zack dug the rolled poster out of his backpack and held it up to the streetlight.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Noah spread his survey sheets across the plywood in aisle six, where the sawdust smelled like pencil shavings. His science fair board needed a frame, two metal brackets, and a strip of tape, but first he had to convince Sahib.

"Three hundred kids," Sahib said, tapping the graph. "The ones who eat breakfast have higher grades. Breakfast makes you smarter. Done. Help me find the brackets."

"It doesn't prove that." Noah picked up a bracket and turned it over. "Two things can go together without one causing the other. Something else could cause both."

"Like what? Magic?"

Noah didn't answer right away. He stared at the graph, at the neat line climbing upward. Then he flipped to his last page, the one with family details some students had volunteered. The breakfast group wasn't random. Their families mostly had higher income, which meant groceries in the house, which meant cereal in the morning and maybe quiet rooms and tutors and all sorts of things he couldn't see. The no-breakfast group was mostly the opposite. Income could be behind both the breakfasts and the grades.

"Correlation," he said out loud, the word Ms. Bui's worksheet had used. "That's what it's called when two things happen together. It doesn't prove cause."

"Fine, detective. Then what's your project? 'Nothing causes anything'?"

"New survey. I ask about breakfast, grades, and income. Then I can check whether income explains both." Noah grabbed the brackets and headed for the register. His stomach growled. He had skipped breakfast to finish the graphs, and he had gotten an A-minus on the last math test, which didn't fit Sahib's neat line at all. He filed that away.

At the register, Ms. Bui from next door was buying a paintbrush. She peered at his graph. "Science fair? My students love those." She tapped the breakfast column. "You know, I haven't eaten breakfast since I was your age. School was easy for me anyway."

Sahib leaned over the counter. "What were your grades?"

"Top of my class, every year," she said, and counted out her change.

Sahib looked at Noah. Noah looked at his graph, where the line climbed so confidently upward, and put the brackets on the belt.

"I'll take the tape too," he said.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
story:
Jasmine pressed her nose against the glass case and stared at the strange flask inside. It had a neck like a swan, curving down and up again before it opened to the air, and beside it a card read: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in these flasks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. Behind her, the science centre hummed with the noise of school groups, and somewhere a presenter was drafting a demonstration about static electricity on a whiteboard.

"There you are," said Auguste, jogging up with Gracie. "Ms. Wilson said we have twenty minutes before the planetarium."

"In a minute," Jasmine said. She couldn't stop looking at the broth in the swan-necked flask. It was clear and pale, and it had been sitting there, according to the card, for weeks.

She thought about her own kitchen at home, two summers ago. She had left a jar of soup on the counter while the family went to the lake, and when they came back the soup was cloudy and sour, while the sealed can beside it stayed fine. She'd blamed her little brother for leaving the lid loose, and they'd argued about it for days. He'd stomped off to his room, and she still hadn't decided whether she owed him an apology, because she'd never figured out what had actually ruined the soup.

"So what's the big deal?" Gracie asked, leaning in. "It's just old soup."

"It's clean soup," Jasmine said. "That's the point. The flask is open, so air can get in, but nothing's growing in it." She traced the curve of the neck with her finger against the glass. "The stuff that spoils broth has to travel through the air, and this bend stops it. It can't get past."

Auguste frowned. "So you think invisible things are floating around and falling into soup?"

"I think that's a guess we could test," Jasmine said. "A hypothesis. If the bend is what's protecting the broth, then a straight-necked flask should go bad, and a bent one shouldn't."

Gracie pointed at a second case down the wall. "Look." A straight-necked flask sat there, its broth clouded and speckled with grey. Jasmine's chest went tight. The two flasks were like an experiment someone had already run for her, and the answer was standing in the glass.

"That's it," she whispered. "The bend matters. The bend is everything."

"So what's your soup story?" Auguste asked.

Jasmine told them about the summer, the open jar, the sealed can. "I blamed him for the lid," she said. "But the lid wasn't the problem. The problem was that the soup was open to the air at all." She wondered whether an apology would fix it, or whether he'd just roll his eyes. She'd find out either way.

"Five minutes!" Ms. Wilson called across the hall, her voice almost infectious with excitement over the planetarium show, which was rumoured to make the whole ceiling appear to spin in one slow revolution.

Jasmine took one last photo of the swan neck on her phone. Then she typed a message to her brother: "Come to the science centre with me Saturday. I'll buy the tickets."

She pressed send.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
The argument started over the bean trays on the windowsill, where three rows of seeds sat folded into damp paper towels inside plastic cups. Marissa pointed at the cup labeled four and said it was obviously the best one, the strongest, the one that would win if the seeds were competing. Alice said that didn't make sense, because a seed couldn't be "the best," and Marissa flipped her ponytail and said Alice just didn't like cup four because it was hers.

"You only like cup one because you planted it," Marissa said. "That's your opinion."

"It's not an opinion," Alice said. "It's a claim. I said beans in the dark cupboard will germinate faster than beans on the windowsill, and that's something we can check."

Ms. Hu, who had been eavesdropping from her desk without looking up, raised one finger. "Evidence, then," she said, and went back to her crossword, which was her way of saying get on with it.

So they set it up. Alice took two cups of beans and put one inside the supply cupboard with the door shut and left the other on the sill beside Marissa's cup four. Alizee, who wanted her own project to win the class fair and had been hovering nearby with her notebook, asked if she could record the data for both trays, because a table of numbers looked impressive on a poster board. Alice agreed, though it stung a little to hand over the part of the experiment that would look best on display day.

By Thursday the cupboard beans had split their coats and shown tiny white hooks, while the sill beans were barely swollen. Alizee wrote the numbers down, measured every sprout twice, and said the difference was real, not a fluke. Marissa stood with her arms crossed, staring at the crooked little sprouts like they had betrayed her personally.

"See," Alice said. "My claim was checkable. The evidence showed it was true. But cup four being the best, that's an opinion. Nobody can test that, because it's just how you feel about it."

Marissa chewed on that for a second. "So I can't be wrong about cup four?"

"You can't be wrong," Alice said, "but you also can't be right."

Marissa laughed despite herself, a short surprised sound, and picked up the cup to give the beans a closer look. The phenomenon of seeds pushing through paper in total darkness was, Ms. Hu remarked on her way past, something botanists had studied for years, and she said the word "phenomenon" the way some people say the word dessert.

On Friday the beans from both trays went into water glasses so the class could watch the sprouts turn green, and Alice noticed that the fattest seed coat, hollow now, floated up buoyant at the top of her glass like a little pale boat. Alizee got her poster board, with the table everyone crowded around to see, and took first place at the fair; Alice's name appeared in the corner in small print. Marissa entered next year with the words "CHECKABLE CLAIM" underlined twice across her display, and cup four, which never sprouted at all, went into the compost bin behind the portable.

"Next time," Marissa said, dropping the empty cup in the sink, "I'm making a claim you can test, and I'm going to win it."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
The elevator in Cameron's new building smelled like burnt popcorn, which at least proved somebody lived there, because everything else about the place looked desolate. Twelve floors of identical brown doors, and behind one of them was apartment 7C, where Cameron now lived, three hundred miles from Oakley and Hanna and every person who already knew him. He dropped his last box on the kitchen counter and made a decision: he would not spend the whole summer friendless. He would find the answer scientifically.

The answer started with a book. His mother had packed it by mistake, a fat orange paperback called The Laws of Everybody, and while unpacking plates he flipped it open to a dog-eared page. In 1950, it said, Leon Festinger and his colleagues studied a student housing complex at MIT, and found that residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them. Not the funniest people. Not the people with the best snacks. The closest ones. Cameron read it twice, then looked at the wall that separated his apartment from 7B.

"Then the math is simple," he told his cat, who supervised the whole operation from the top of the fridge, blinking slowly, as cats do. "Door across the hall, door next door, door below. Test subjects one, two, and three." He wrote their locations on a napkin, because real scientists always wrote things down, and marched into the hall.

Subject one, across the hall, was a girl with purple headphones who opened her door exactly four inches. "What," she said.

"Hi, I'm Cameron, I live in 7C, and according to Festinger we're statistically required to be friends."

She stared. He heard music leaking from her headphones, something with a lot of voltage in the guitars. "Fes-who?"

"Festinger. 1950. Housing complex at MIT. He found people became friends with whoever lived closest." He pointed at his door. "That's me. Closest."

"Wow, you really are the worst scientist," she said, but she was almost smiling. "Maya. Seven-D. I'm not even in your study, I'm catty-corner."

"Noted." He made a mark on the napkin. "You're a control group."

"Am I a good one?"

"The best." He was pretty sure control groups couldn't be good or bad, but arguing with her already felt like something Oakley would do, and that made his chest hurt in a good way.

Subject two, in 7B, turned out to be an ancient man named Mr. Mwangi who offered him tea and beat him at checkers twice. Subject three, the kid downstairs, was at camp all summer, an obvious flaw in the experiment. Cameron reported his findings that night on a video call, holding up the napkin while Hanna and Oakley squinted at it through the screen.

"Wait," Hanna said. "You made a friend by citing an old study at her?"

"Seven-zero, Maya calls it," Cameron said. "She's coming over Friday to supervise my checkers rematch with Mr. Mwangi. She thinks he cheats."

"Everybody cheats at checkers," Oakley said. "Tell her the voltage guy downstairs says hi."

"He's at camp, Oakley."

"Tell him anyway."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
story:
The flashlight in Noah's hand was the only thing standing between him and a failing grade. Ms. Wang had made it clear: everyone had to explain, at the science fair table tomorrow, why Earth has seasons, and his last attempt had gone so badly that even the beakers seemed embarrassed for him.

"Tell me again what you said," Kareem said, leaning against the lab table while Ms. Wang supervised the after-school setup across the room.

"I said summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun," Noah admitted.

Kaeden winced. "You said that. Out loud. In front of her."

"She didn't even react at first. She just stood there, holding a marker, looking at me like a clock that had stopped."

That moment had replayed in Noah's head all night. He'd been so sure. Closer meant warmer; that was obvious. But when he'd said it, Ms. Wang had only written two words on the board and underlined them twice: "angle" and "tilt." Then she'd told him he could try again tomorrow at his table, and that his exhibit had better show something real.

Now he stood in the tranquil, half-dark science room after everyone else had gone home, staring at a globe, a flashlight, and a bowl of sand he'd grabbed as his "ground." A plastic boat sat in it, leftover from some younger kid's project; the little vessel had been sailing across the sand all afternoon, going nowhere.

"Move the boat, sailor," Kaeden said, flicking it out of the way.

Noah switched on the flashlight and pointed it straight down at the sand. A small, bright circle glowed there, sharp-edged and intense. Then, slowly, he tilted the flashlight. The circle stretched into a long oval, and the glow went dim and pale, like the light was spreading itself too thin.

"Whoa," Kareem said quietly. "Look at that."

"The same light," Noah murmured, tilting it further, watching the oval grow wider and dimmer still, "spread over more ground."

He kept the flashlight tilted and held his hand above the sand, then straightened the beam again. The small circle felt hotter. He tested it once more, tilted and straight, tilted and straight, because he did not trust a thing he had only seen once.

"So when our part of Earth is tilted toward the sun," Noah said slowly, grabbing the globe and turning its axis, "the sunlight comes down straighter, like this." He held the beam perpendicular to the globe's surface. "Summer. Same amount of light packed onto a smaller piece of ground, so it heats up more."

"And when we're tilted away?" Kaeden asked.

Noah angled the beam. The light smeared across a whole hemisphere, weak and thin. "Winter. Same light, spread thin."

Kareem frowned. "So it's not about distance at all?"

"Distance has nothing to do with it. It's the tilt." Noah laughed, a short, disbelieving burst. "I argued about that for ten minutes yesterday."

"You argued with confidence," Kaeden said. "That's the scary part."

Ms. Wang drifted over, looked at the bright circle, the wide dim oval, and the tilted globe, and raised one eyebrow at the plastic boat Noah was setting upright in the sand. "And what exactly is that vessel demonstrating?"

"Nothing," Noah said. "It's supervising me."

She almost smiled. "Tomorrow, start with the flashlight. Lead with that."

"Ms. Wang," Noah said, holding the beam straight down until the sand glowed in one fierce little circle, "watch this part."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A "parking lot" is a list where a meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item.
story:
Declan tapped the agenda paper against his knee and counted the faces in the circle. Six members of the robotics club, all of them still in track shorts because the meeting happened right after practice, in the corner of the gym while Mr. Suzuki put away the hurdles. He had volunteered to run today's meeting because nobody else wanted to, and now he wondered if he had made a mistake.

"First item," he read. "Fundraising for the regional competition." He had barely finished the sentence when Maxim's hand shot up.

"What if we built a robot that delivers snacks to classrooms? People would pay for that. We could charge two dollars a delivery." Maxim leaned forward, elbows on knees, and Izabella immediately jumped in about which hallway would be fastest. Within a minute, half the group was designing snack routes and nobody had said a word about fundraising. Declan looked at his agenda and noticed a pattern he hadn't expected: every meeting went this way. Somebody's exciting idea arrived, and the whole agenda collapsed like a dropped stack of plates. Was the problem the people, or was there something about how the meeting itself worked?

He raised his voice just enough to be heard over the squeak of sneakers. "Hold on. Maxim, that idea might be great, but it's not what we're working on right now." Then he did something he'd seen a coach do once with complaints: he wrote it down. At the top of a fresh page he printed SNACK ROBOT and drew a box around it. "This is our parking lot," he said. "A list where I write down off-topic ideas so we can discuss them later instead of derailing the current item."

Maxim frowned. "So it just sits there?"

"It gets discussed at the end, or next meeting. You'll get your turn." Declan hadn't planned that promise, but saying it out loud made sense to him. If people trusted the box, maybe they'd let go of the topic without a fight.

They got through fundraising in eleven minutes, which felt like a record. When someone started on the snack robot again, Declan pointed at the box, and she stopped. He caught Izabella watching him the way she watched a good robot run, like she was trying to figure out which gear was doing the work.

At the end he read the parking lot out loud. Maxim's idea went first, and it turned out to have a real use: they could propose it to the student council as a service project. "Funny," Izabella said as they folded chairs. "Writing it down made it bigger, not smaller."

Mr. Suzuki called from the equipment room, "Declan, you left your agenda sheet on the bleachers."

He went to get it, and under the parking lot box, in Maxim's handwriting, was a new entry: Declan for club president?

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
William spread the two graphs on the picnic table, pinning the corners with pinecones because the wind would not cooperate. One graph showed a desert, with temperature bars climbing high and rainfall bars so short they looked like mistakes. The other showed a rainforest, where the rainfall bars towered over everything. He had promised Ms. Romano he would finish the comparison on the trip, and tonight was the last night.

"Which one's the desert?" Rosalie asked, sliding onto the bench beside him with her mug of cocoa. Deegan sat across the table, spinning the small globe he had brought for the astronomy unit.

"Guess," William said, and she pointed at the rainfall bars immediately.

"That one's the rainforest. But how can both places be hot? That's the part I don't get." She tapped the temperature lines. "Look, the desert is hotter sometimes, but the rainforest gets wet all year. Something has to explain the difference, right? Rain doesn't just happen or not happen for no reason."

Deegan stopped spinning the globe and frowned at it. "Hey, wait." He dragged his finger across it. "Sahara. Arabian. Australian. They're all lined up. There's a whole belt of them up here, and another belt down here. What are the odds?"

William leaned over. The deserts really did line up, two ragged rings around the globe. "Where's that, exactly? On the latitude lines." They found the equator, then counted up the marked lines. The big deserts sat near thirty degrees north, and the southern ones near thirty degrees south.

"So they're at thirty degrees," Rosalie said slowly. "But that's a location, not a reason. The graphs don't show why."

William turned the globe to the equator and squinted at the green band across South America and Africa. "What's the air doing there, though? At the equator it rains and rains, and everything thrives, jungle everywhere. At thirty degrees, dry. It's like the air itself is different, but we can't see air. How do you test something invisible?" He sat back, thinking. His Achilles tendon ached from the morning hike, and he rolled his ankle in circles while he stared at the two graphs side by side.

"Conventional wisdom would just say 'some places are dry,'" Deegan said, "and that's boring."

"Then let's not be conventional," William said. He flipped his graph paper over and drew two quick sketches: a rising arrow over the equator's rainforest, and a sinking arrow over the desert belt at thirty degrees north and thirty degrees south. "Rising air over the equator. Sinking air over the deserts. If sinking air warms up and dries out, that's the cause, and the rainfall bars prove it. Deserts near thirty degrees, rainforests at the equator. It fits everything on the globe."

Rosalie grabbed the pencil. "Then label it before the wind takes it."

"Label what?" Ms. Romano asked, walking over from the fire with the kettle.

William held up the sketch. "The reason the deserts line up in two belts. Thirty degrees north and south, where sinking air warms up and dries out."

Ms. Romano smiled and set down the kettle. "Show me the rainfall bars again."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Charlie had exactly one goal for Saturday afternoon: get onto ClipVerse, where Giselle and Ariane had been posting videos of their hamster, Biscuit, for two whole weeks. She settled at the desk in the den, typed her username, her email, and then hit the question she'd been dreading. Date of birth. She entered her real birthday, and the screen went red. "You must be 13 or older to create an account."

She stared at it. Giselle was thirteen in October, and Ariane had turned thirteen in March, so that explained them. But why thirteen? Nobody chose thirteen for anything. Thirteen was a weird age, not sweet sixteen, not eighteen, not even a nice symmetrical number like twelve.

She tried a small experiment, the way her science teacher Ms. Abdi taught them to test a hypothesis. She made up a birthday, one that made her fourteen, and clicked submit. The account page opened instantly, cheerful and green. So it wasn't that the site cared about her actual age; it only cared what she typed. Charlie closed the tab without saving, because it felt like lying, even to a machine. Instead she opened a search window and typed, why do websites make you be 13.

The answer appeared in a paragraph she read twice. Something called the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, from 1998, required parental consent before websites collected personal information from children under 13. That was why so many sites required users to be 13. It wasn't a rule ClipVerse made up; it was a law, older than her mom's car.

She called Giselle, who answered mid-chew. "Biscuit escaped into the couch again," Giselle said. "My dad diagnosed it as a carnivore problem. He thinks Biscuit is hunting crumbs." Charlie laughed, then asked, "Did you have to get your mom's permission when you signed up? Because of the law thing?" There was a pause, and the sound of a couch cushion being lifted. "She typed something. I thought she was just being nosy. Hang on, Ariane's here, I'm putting you on speaker."

Ariane's voice crackled through. "Wait, is that why it kept asking for my birthday three times? I thought it was broken." Charlie explained what she'd found, keeping it short, and heard Giselle yell to her mom in the background, "MOM, WAS THAT THE PRIVACY LAW?" A distant voice said something about 1998 and a form.

"Come over," Giselle said. "We'll film Biscuit's escape and put your name in the caption. You can be the producer until you're officially old."

"Nine months," Charlie said.

"Nine months," Giselle agreed, and something small and furry squeaked on the other end.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so a wire's resistance is found by dividing the voltage across it by the current through it.
story:
The skate park at five o'clock was all shadows and squeaking wheels, and Anna had claimed the shady corner under the halfpipe where a strip of lush grass had somehow survived the whole summer. She spread out her science-fair supplies on a folded towel: a battery, a coil of thin copper wire, a breadboard, and Mikael's multimeter, which they had promised to return without scratches, drool, or regret. Neil arrived on his board, skidded to a stop, and dropped a notebook on the grass.

"You forgot to document the readings again," Mikael said, without even looking up.

"I did not forget," Neil said. "I camouflaged them. I wrote them in green pen. On the grass-stain page. It's a system."

Anna flipped through the notebook, found two numbers hiding in a smear of green ink, and held them up like evidence at a trial. "Two point four volts across the wire. Zero point one two amps through it. That's all we measured before the meter battery died." Their whole project was due Monday, and the one number they actually needed, the resistance of that wire, was still missing. The fair judges wanted all three numbers, not two and a hopeful shrug.

She stared at the wire, which just sat there looking innocent, as if it had no properties at all. "The resistance is in there somewhere," she muttered. "We just can't see it. It's like the wire is wearing camouflage." Then she remembered Ms. González saying one sentence before shooing them out of the lab to go enjoy the weekend. Ohm's law, she had called it: voltage equals current times resistance. Anna said it out loud twice, and the second time she heard it click into place. If voltage equals current times resistance, then resistance had to be voltage divided by current. She grabbed the notebook.

"Two point four divided by zero point one two," she said, doing it longhand in the margin because her phone was dead, which Neil found hilarious for reasons he refused to explain. Mikael leaned over her shoulder and counted the decimal moves with his finger, hovering an inch from the page as if touching it might change the answer. "Twenty," Anna announced. "Twenty ohms. The wire was hiding twenty ohms this entire time and giggling about it."

Neil wrote it down in green pen, on a fresh page, underlined three times. Then he stood, dropped his board on the concrete, and said, "To celebrate, you two are going to watch me land a kickflip, and I am going to document the landing. In pen. No camouflage."

"Wear a helmet," Mikael called after him. "Ohm's law does not cover your head."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Charlie stood backstage in the gymnasium, clutching her word list so tightly that the paper had gone soft at the edges. Row after row of folded bleachers rattled as students from six schools filed in, and the microphone at center court gave a sharp squeal that made half the audience laugh.

She had reread the list every night for two weeks, all four hundred words, until her eyes ached. Last night, sitting at the kitchen table, she had complained about it, and her dad had set down his coffee and told her about a study he had read at work. "In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it," he said. "So instead of rereading the list again, I'm going to quiz you out loud." Charlie had groaned, but she had spelled sixty words at him while he stirred the pasta sauce and got tomato on the corner of the page, right next to "chrysanthemum."

She remembered that now because round two had just knocked out Elle, who froze on "borough" and whispered "b-u-r-r-o" into the mic. Elle walked offstage with her chin up, but her chin trembled on the way. Izaiah was still in, mouthing each word to himself before speaking, and Ms. Qureshi, the librarian who ran the bee, kept score on a tall clipboard like a judge at a gymnastics meet.

"Contestant fourteen, your word is 'temporary,'" Ms. Qureshi said.

Charlie's stomach dropped. Then, oddly, the word felt familiar in her mouth, like a hallway she had walked before. Last night her dad had quizzed her on that exact word, and she had missed it, adding an extra "p" because she was laughing at something he said about the pasta sauce. He had made her spell it again, then twice more, and she had griped that it was a waste of time. She said it now, letter by letter, and Ms. Qureshi nodded. "Correct."

Two rounds later, three spellers remained. Izaiah retired to his seat after tangling himself up in "liaison," applauding the kid who beat him, and Charlie got "context," which she had also spelled out loud at the kitchen table, standing on one foot for no reason anyone could defend. The letters came out steady. Correct again.

Now the gym was quieter, just her and a seventh grader in a green hoodie. Ms. Qureshi leaned toward the microphone. "Contestant fourteen, your word is 'chrysanthemum.'" Charlie glanced down at the list still folded in her hand, at the faint orange smudge beside the word, and closed her eyes. She could see the tomato sauce. She could hear her dad's voice asking it. "C," she began, "h..."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Hudson stared at the duffel bag on his bed, the one he had inherited from his older brother, still smelling faintly of the summer Cole had spent at the same camp. In two weeks Hudson would leave for three weeks of canoes and campfires, and everyone kept saying it would be the best time of his life. The trouble was that Hudson had never set foot in a canoe, and last Saturday at the lake with his class he had nearly flipped one just getting in. Dyson had laughed so hard he fell off the dock, and Farrah had to grip Hudson's sleeve to keep him from going under. He did not want to spend three weeks being the boy who swamped the boat.

So he came up with a plan. Mr. Carvalho, the neighbour across the fence, kept an old green canoe on sawhorses behind his garage, and he said Hudson could borrow it as long as he brought it back clean. Hudson dragged it into his own backyard, set it on two plastic lawn chairs, and climbed in wearing the life jacket he'd been issued early from the camp packing list. He started at the gunwale, the way he had at the lake, one foot on the edge. The canoe tipped so fast he had to grab the grass.

He tried again, this time in the middle, knees bent, weight low, and the boat sat under him like a stubborn dog that had finally decided to cooperate. He stepped out onto the edge, and over it went; he crouched in the center, and it held steady. He did it four more times, calling out the results, while Dyson took notes on his phone like it was a lab experiment. "Middle and low, stable," Dyson read back. "Side, faceplant." It was almost ironic, Hudson thought, that the dangerous part wasn't the paddling at all, it was the five seconds of climbing aboard.

Farrah showed up after lunch with a bag of chips and a theory. "My brain is full of these facts from camp brochures," she said, "and I read this science thing about how a neuron fires faster every time you repeat a movement. So basically your body is memorizing the step before your head does." Hudson wasn't sure that was exactly how it worked, but he liked the idea. He climbed in and out eleven more times until his legs ached and the motion felt as ordinary as climbing stairs.

On the last night before camp, he returned the canoe scrubbed and rinsed, and Mr. Carvalho asked how the practice had gone. "I only fell twice," Hudson said, shouldering the duffel. "Ask me again in three weeks."

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him.
story:
The presentation was due tomorrow, and Dylan still had nothing but a page of notes that read "Treaty of Versailles, then somehow WWII?" He spread his books across the library table and stared at them like they might arrange themselves.

"Move over," Maxton said, dropping into the chair beside him with a wrapped burrito. "Food's prohibited in here, by the way, so keep your voice down."

"Then why'd you bring it?"

"Because Mr. Dela Cruz is at the desk and he likes me. Watch." Maxton unwrapped it slowly. The librarian glanced over, then went back to his computer. Maxton grinned. "See? Nothing happened."

Dylan went back to his notes. The Treaty of Versailles had prohibited Germany from keeping troops in the Rhineland, a strip along its western edge. That was the rule. In March 1936, Hitler had sent troops in anyway. Dylan read the next line twice: Britain and France did not use force to stop him. He looked up.

"That's it," he said.

"What's it?"

"That's the answer to my whole question." He tapped the page. "The treaty said no troops there. Hitler put troops there anyway. And nobody stopped him." He stopped, frowning. "But how does that lead to a whole war?"

Maxton leaned back, chewing. "Dunno. Ask Amelie, she actually reads."

Amelie was at the next table with her headphones on, but she pulled one off when Dylan slid into the chair across from her. He laid out the facts like cards. The treaty made a rule. Hitler broke the rule in March 1936. Britain and France had armies, bigger ones, and they did nothing.

"So they let him," Amelie said.

"Right. But why does letting him once matter?"

Amelie shrugged, then glanced over Dylan's shoulder. Maxton was no longer at the table. He was at the far shelf by the window, and he was sliding a book into his backpack. Not checking it out. Taking it.

"He did that because you let the burrito go," Amelie said quietly.

Dylan watched. Maxton zipped the bag, casual, like a person who has learned that rules in this library are decorative. Something clicked in Dylan's head so hard he almost said it out loud. You let one rule break, and the next rule break gets easier, and bigger.

He stood up. "Maxton. Put it back."

"Why? Nobody stopped me before."

"Put it back or I tell Mr. Dela Cruz. I'm serious."

Maxton studied him, then walked back to the shelf, slid the book out of the bag, and shelved it upside down. He sat down and unwrapped a second burrito from his pocket, and this time Mr. Dela Cruz rose from the desk and came toward them, keys jingling, unhurried.

"So did you figure out your presentation?" Maxton asked, chewing.

"Yeah," Dylan said. "I actually think I did."

"Good," said Mr. Dela Cruz, arriving at the table. "Then you can explain it to me while I write up your friend."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
story:
Stella stood at the kitchen window while her grandmother rolled the last of the date pastries, because tomorrow might be Eid, and tomorrow might not. The whole day hung on a sliver of moon nobody had seen yet. Her little brother had spent the evening trying to ridicule her method, saying that a fourteen-year-old with a pair of binoculars could not possibly out-predict the mosque announcement, but Stella had a theory and she intended to test it.

"Grandma, how do they decide?" she asked.

Grandma dusted flour from her hands. "Someone must see the new crescent, Stella. The month ends when the eye catches it."

That was the hidden part, Stella thought. Ramadan had run its course like a siege, thirty days of holding the line, no food or water from the first pale light of dawn until the sky went dark at sunset. A whole month of it, and its ending depended on something as thin as a fingernail clipping low in the sky. If the crescent appeared tonight, Eid al-Fitr would come tomorrow with the visiting and the feasting. If clouds hid it, everyone would wait another day, and the pastries would sit under their cloth getting stale.

After dinner, when the sky over the rooftops turned the color of molten copper, Stella climbed the stairs to the little balcony with the binoculars and a notebook. She had written down the time of sunset from the calendar, and she meant to watch the western horizon for exactly forty minutes, because she had read that a young moon sets soon after the sun does. If she saw nothing in that window, the moon was either too faint or not there yet. At minute thirty-two, just above the chimney of the house across the lane, she caught it: a curved thread of light, so thin it seemed like a scratch on the sky.

She was down the stairs in seconds, notebook waving. "I saw it! Low, in the west, right where it should be!"

Her brother folded his arms. "That could have been anything."

"Then call the mosque and ask if anyone else reported it."

Before he could argue, the phone rang in the hall, and Stella heard her father's voice rise with delight. Grandma lifted the cloth off the pastries and smiled. Noemi and Eleni were coming over in the morning, and Stella was already planning to meet them at the door with the dates first, before anything else, because after a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, that was the proper way to begin.

"Tell Noemi to come early," she called to her father. "I want her to see the table before we eat all of it."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under first-past-the-post, votes for losing candidates in a district elect no one, which is why they are sometimes called wasted votes.
story:
Amelia had assumed her first visit to city hall would be boring until she spotted the folding tables set up in the lobby with ballots, a shoebox for each paper district, and a hand-lettered sign reading Sample Election: Everyone Votes Twice. Ms. Friedman, whose civics club met on Thursdays, was weighing the shoeboxes with a kitchen scale. "First vote is first-past-the-post," she announced. "One winner per district. Second vote we pool everyone's ballots and split the seats proportionally. Amelia, you're the recorder."

Amelia sat down between Alan and Tess and started tallying. In District One, the Amber party took 41 percent, Teal took 39, and Lilac took 20, so Amber's candidate won the single seat. Tess, counting beside her, frowned at her page. "I voted Lilac here," she said quietly. "Twenty people's ballots and we got nothing to show for it."

"My grandpa says that all the time," Alan said, stacking the Lilac ballots into a neat pile. "Says his vote never counts in his district, every single year." Amelia looked at the pile, then at the shoebox, then at the pile again. It was like guessing at something hidden: the ballots hadn't vanished, but they had elected no one, and that had to be the reason her grandpa felt invisible. She tested it against District Two, where Teal had lost by a whisker, and District Three, where Lilac had lost badly. Same result in every box. "These are wasted votes," she said. "That's what they're called, right? Votes for losing candidates in a district elect no one." Ms. Friedman looked over and nodded once, then went back to her scale.

For the second vote, everything went into one giant tub, and the seats came out in shares that matched the percentages almost exactly. Lilac, shut out three times before, suddenly held two seats, and Amelia felt the cumulative effect of all those "useless" ballots turning into real representation at once. It was satisfying, like watching scattered coins add up. But when Amber's total slipped from three seats to two, Alan groaned. "So my party loses a seat just because the system changes?" He tried to negotiate a recount, offering to recount the tub himself, but the totals held.

Afterward, the three of them sat on the wide front steps of city hall while Ms. Friedman carried the shoeboxes out to her car. Tess tore a corner off her ballot and folded it into a tiny Lilac flag. "Our system isn't broken," Amelia said slowly, turning her tally sheet over. "It just does a thing nobody told us it was doing."

Alan squinted at the little flag. "So which one do we actually use?"

Tess planted the flag between the concrete seams of the step and said, "Guess I'll ask my grandpa. He's got forty years of proof it's the other one."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
story:
The scoreboard flashed a trivia question between quarters, and Jacob read it twice before nudging Chelsea's arm. "Why does the big game use Roman numerals instead of regular numbers? First correct answer to section 212 wins a team jacket."

Chelsea pulled out her phone. "Easy. I'll look it up."

"You can't," Brogan said, pointing at the screen above the field. "No phones for the trivia contest. They said it at the start. One guess per section, out loud, to the usher."

The usher was already climbing the steps toward them, holding a clipboard. Jacob's dad leaned over from the next row. "Well? Somebody answer the man. There's a jacket on the line."

"I is just one," Brogan said quickly. "Super Bowl I. Because it was the first one, right? So they called it that from the beginning."

Something about that felt wrong to Jacob, though he couldn't have said why at first. He stared at the Roman numerals scrolling along the scoreboard rim, LXIII, LXIV, the numbers marching past in gold. If the game had been named Super Bowl I at the start, the question would be pointless. Contest questions had answers that surprised people. He tried a different idea: the name came later. If nobody called it that at the time, then what did they call it?

The usher reached their row. "Section 212, I need your answer."

"Hold on," Jacob said. "One second." He thought about his grandfather, who complained every February that the game had a boring name when he was young. Not "the Super Bowl." Something long and official, the kind of name a committee would invent. Two leagues, back then, playing each other. The AFL and the NFL.

"The first one wasn't called Super Bowl I," Jacob said. "The Roman numeral got added later. Its official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game."

The usher checked his clipboard. "That's the answer." He wrote something down and gave Jacob a red voucher. "Pick up the jacket at guest services after the fourth quarter."

Brogan stared at him. "How did you know that?"

"My grandpa. He used to call it the championship game, never the Super Bowl, and I always figured he was just being vague about it on purpose. Turns out that's what it was actually called." Jacob looked at the voucher, then folded it into his pocket.

"Total bias," Brogan said. "You had a grandfather advantage."

"Take it up with the scoreboard."

Chelsea leaned back in her seat, shaking her head. "I'm never trusting Roman numerals again."

On the field the teams lined up for the second-half kickoff, and the whole stadium stood up as the roar did not cease but climbed, wave after wave, until the ball went sailing into the lights.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The list was taped to the gym door by first period, and Alexandra read it twice before the bell. Rhett first in scoring average, Charlie fourth, her own name nowhere in the top ten. She had started every game, though, and she was the one who kept the loose balls alive. Last spring her uncle had leaned over a plate of nachos at the sports bar while a game flickered on the screen behind him and said that the 2003 book "Moneyball," by Michael Lewis, described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players. Rich teams spent huge money; the A's found players the rankings missed. She had thought it was just a story about baseball. Now she stood in the hallway wondering what the list on the gym door actually measured, and what it left out.

In math class she wrote the question at the top of her notebook. Scoring average counted only baskets, but a basket needed someone to pass the ball and someone to grab the rebound. Those things were real, they just weren't on the list. She had an idea, and it was small enough to test. She took the scoresheet from the last three games out of her binder and started a tally column of her own: passes that led directly to a shot, recovered rebounds, times she drew the defender away from Charlie under the hoop.

Charlie found her at lunch doing it, chin on her fist, pencil hovering. "That looks like homework for a class we don't take."

"It's the other half of the game," Alexandra said. She spun the paper toward him. Charlie squinted, then went quiet in a way he almost never did. In the second column he saw the number beside her name, and beside it, in her handwriting, three small tallies from a game he remembered because he'd been flat with a sinus infection and on antibiotics all week, dizzy and slow, and she had carried the passing that night. The scoring average had shown none of it. He'd felt invisible that week too, and so had she, and neither of them had said so.

By Friday, fourteen kids had signed the sheet of paper Alexandra slid across the desk in Mr. Park's room. It was a petition, short and blunt: include passing and rebound tallies in the season summary, not just points. Mr. Park read it, then looked up over his glasses.

"You know the coach picks the list," he said. "You know he might say no."

Alexandra nodded. Rhett appeared in the doorway with his bag over one shoulder, glapping the doorframe with his palm. "Did he look at the numbers?" Rhett asked.

Mr. Park picked up his pen and turned to the last page, where the tallies ran in neat rows down the margin.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Zoey flipped the switch on her remote-control truck, and nothing happened. Again. She'd charged the battery all night in the garage workshop, and it was dead by morning. That made three times this week.

"Something's draining it," she told Clarke, who was sprawled on the workbench with a screwdriver in his hand. "I can't see what, but something is."

"Maybe the battery's just broken," Clarke said. "Your drain idea is just a theory."

Zoey shook her head so fast her ponytail whipped around. "No. A theory isn't a guess. A theory is an explanation that's been tested over and over and it keeps working. What I have is a hypothesis. A hypothesis is an idea still being tested. That's the whole difference." She'd picked that up at the science centre last month, when a guide had corrected her on almost the exact same mistake, and she'd never forgotten it.

"Fine, Your Majesty," Clarke said, holding up the screwdriver like a tiny sword. "Test your hypothesis, then. Though I should warn you, this garage is not a monarchy. You can't just declare things by royal decree."

"I decree nothing," Zoey said. "I test things." She unscrewed the truck's battery cover, clipped a small flashlight bulb into the circuit between the battery and the truck, and switched everything off. If nothing was draining the battery, the bulb should stay dark. If something hidden was pulling current even when the truck was "off," the bulb would glow. She set it on the bench, and the two of them leaned in close, noses almost touching the wires.

For a long moment the bulb sat dark, and Zoey felt her hypothesis wobble. Then a faint orange thread appeared in the glass, steadied, and brightened. Something inside the truck was definitely sipping power even when it was switched off. Clarke whooped and nearly knocked over a jar of screws.

"The receiver board," Zoey said, tracing the wire with a diligent finger, slow and careful now, checking every connection before she touched anything. "Look, the solder's bridged two pads. It's always on. The switch never actually cuts it out." Her dad had built this truck years ago, and someday she would inherit all his tools and half-finished projects, but right now she was glad this one had landed in her hands early. She fetched the soldering iron, waited for it to heat, and touched it to the tiny blob of solder while Clarke held the board steady.

She rebuilt the circuit, reconnected the battery, and left the bulb in place. They watched it together. Ten seconds. Thirty. A full minute, and the glass stayed completely, beautifully dark.

"Told you," Zoey said, and grinned at the little unlit bulb glowing with nothing at all.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Jackson had forty minutes before his bus came, and one mall food court table to himself, which was why he kept checking his phone instead of eating his pretzel. Two nights ago he had posted a photo of his dog wearing a paper hat, and underneath it he had written, "Hanging at the Riverside Mall, table by the pretzel place, 4:30ish." His account was private. Only people he had accepted could see it. That was supposed to mean it stayed with friends.

The comment had come in this morning, from an account called hawkboy_99 that Jackson did not recognize at all. "cool dog. is that the table near the smoothie stand? i'll be there sometime." Jackson read it four times during math while Mr. Carvalho summarized the chapter on early agriculture, and he absorbed none of it. Now he sat with his back to the escalator, watching faces.

Rae slid into the seat across from him, dropping a bag from the shoe store. "You look like you're guarding state secrets. Or a pretzel."

"Someone I don't know commented on my post. My account's private." He turned the phone around.

Rae frowned at the screen. The food court smelled like cinnamon and warm soft pretzel, and the noise of the escalator rose and fell behind them. "You sure you never accepted them? Scroll your followers."

They scrolled together. Halfway down the list, past a cousin, past Rocco, Jackson found hawkboy_99. The name tapped a memory: a guy from summer day camp, two years ago, who had sent a request and Jackson had tapped accept without thinking, the way you hand someone a pencil.

"So they're a follower," Rae said. "Private just limits who can see your posts. Anyone you already accepted can still copy or share what they see."

Jackson tested it right there. He took a screenshot of his own dog post, then forwarded it to Rocco with the words, "could you post this if I asked?" Rocco, standing in line at the smoothie stand three tables away, held up his phone, gave a thumbs up, and Jackson watched his own photo appear on Rocco's public account within thirty seconds. Anyone in the world could see it now. Anyone at all could know exactly which table he sat at on Thursdays.

His bus was in ten minutes. Jackson tapped settings, removed hawkboy_99, and deleted the post, but the screenshot already lived on Rocco's page, and there was no way to reach into everyone's phones and pull it back. He slid the phone into his pocket and picked up his cold pretzel.

"Coming?" Rae asked, already standing.

Jackson looked once more at the escalator, at all the strangers riding down past the pretzel sign. "Yeah," he said. "Let's take the other exit."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
The disputed call came with two minutes left in the fourth quarter. Grandpa's living room was full: Carter, his friends Ralph and Salim, Grandpa, and an uncle who had claimed the recliner by halftime. The receiver caught the ball at the sideline, or maybe he didn't, and the whole room started shouting at once. Then the screen cut to a replay, and everyone leaned forward.

"He was in," Salim said.

"His toe was on the line. Look at it," Ralph said.

The replay ran three times in slow motion. The room voted, argued, voted again, and finally agreed the catch counted. Then the uncle leaned back and said, "You know, when I was a kid, we would have just fought about it until the game was over. Nobody would ever know."

Carter looked at him. "What do you mean? TV always shows replays."

"Not always," the uncle said. "Somebody had to be first."

That idea stuck in Carter's head for the rest of the quarter, and he kept turning it over while Ralph and Salim argued about whether the kicker was any good. If replays had a first time, then there was a specific game, a specific day, when a director tried it once and everything after that was different. The problem was that the moment itself was gone. You couldn't watch a broadcast from before instant replay and see what TV looked like without it, at least not the whole picture. It was like trying to prove the rule of a game by watching people play before the rule existed.

Carter pulled out his phone at the commercial break and searched. He found it fast, but the first page was vague, just "some game in the sixties," and a second page seemed to contradict it with a different year. He scrolled until two sources agreed. Then he checked the date against a third one, because a contradiction meant somebody was wrong, and he wanted to know who.

"Grandpa," Carter said, "do you remember where you were on December 7, 1963?"

Grandpa squinted at him. "I was thirteen. Why?"

"Because that's when it happened. The Army-Navy game. A CBS director named Tony Verna used instant replay in a live sports broadcast for the first time. That was the first one ever."

The uncle sat up in the recliner. "Army-Navy. I've heard that. That's the one."

"So you were the same age I am now," Carter said, "when the first replay ever showed up on TV."

Grandpa was quiet for a second, watching the screen where the kicker was lining up. "I didn't know it was first. I just knew that one season we argued and the next season we pointed at the set." He turned the volume up. "Kick's coming. Watch close, because you're only going to get to see it live once, and then you're going to get to see it forever."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
The outfield grass was still wet when Mr. Kaminski clicked his stopwatch and pointed at the foul poles. "Two laps around the whole diamond," he said. "Eight hundred metres. Tryouts end at noon, so this is your one shot today." Henry crouched at the backstop beside Heinrich, who was bouncing on his toes like a piston, ready to explode.

The whistle blew and Heinrich took off like the fence was on fire. Henry forced himself to hold back, even when Rebekah, stretching by first base, called out, "Heinrich's already ten steps up!" Henry kept his own count, the one he had practiced all week: not fast, not slow, a rhythm he thought he could hold twice. Around second base, around third, Heinrich hit the lap mark flying while Henry crossed it three seconds behind, feeling annoyingly fresh.

The second lap changed everything. Heinrich's legs, which had portrayed pure speed on the first circuit, now looked heavy and confused, as if they belonged to someone else. He shortened, then shortened again, and by the time they came out of the turn into the final straight, Henry was on his shoulder. Heinrich's arms were windmilling. "Go," Heinrich gasped, and Henry went, passing him clean and leaning through the finish.

Mr. Kaminski stopped the watch and showed Henry the split. "Your two laps are almost identical. That's what I want to see." Henry walked back and put a hand on Heinrich's back while Heinrich stood with his hands on his knees. "I burned everything in the first lap," Heinrich said. "I had nothing left." Henry nodded.
