"Same thing happened to me last week. I went out hard, then I slowed way down on the second one, like my legs just quit. Somebody passed me right at the end, just like I passed you."

Heinrich straightened up, still breathing hard. "So the trick is not going as fast as you can at the start?" "The trick," Henry said, "is going the fastest speed you can still hold for both laps. It has to be one coherent pace, not two different races." Mr. Kaminski checked his clipboard. "Heinrich, the backup group runs at eleven thirty. That's your second chance." Heinrich looked at the clock on the scoreboard, then at the track of flattened grass ringing the diamond. "Okay," he said. "This time I'm staying with you."

Rebekah tossed Henry his water bottle from the fence, and Heinrich was already jogging to the backstop to wait for the whistle.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and old vinyl by the time it rolled through the gates of Hartwell Living History Farm, where people in bonnets and suspenders pretended it was still 1852. Lea pressed her forehead to the window. She had wanted this trip all month, mostly because of one rumor: the farm let visitors collect eggs from the chicken yard.

Ms. Wanjiru counted heads twice, then handed out activity sheets. "Free exploration for forty minutes," she said. "Stay in sight of the big barn." Lea was already moving, with Eliza and Gage trailing behind her, past a woman churning butter and a man who insisted on calling the farm's ox "His Majesty," like the whole barnyard was a monarchy and the ox sat on the throne.

The chicken yard was loud and dusty, and a woman in a striped apron handed Gage a woven basket. "Six eggs," she said, "from the nests along the fence." Gage crouched by the first nest, lifted a brown egg into the basket, and then froze. He looked around the yard, squinting at every feathered body. "Wait. There's no rooster anywhere. None of these are big ones with the tail feathers. So if I put these eggs somewhere warm, would they hatch?"

Eliza shrugged. "Probably? That's how chicks happen, right? Egg, then warm, then chick."

Lea watched the hens scratching in the dust. Something about the question snagged in her mind. If eggs needed a rooster to become chicks, then every egg a hen ever laid would need one, and hens here were laying eggs with no rooster in the yard at all. Did the hens even know the difference? She turned the idea over. Maybe the hens laid eggs no matter what, and the rooster only mattered for what came after. "I don't think they'd hatch," she said slowly. "I think hens lay eggs whether or not there's a rooster. But without a rooster, the eggs can't turn into chicks. They're just eggs."

"That's a big claim," Eliza said. "Can you justify it, or are you guessing?"

"There's a test," Lea said. She asked the woman in the striped apron, "Do you keep a rooster in this yard?" The woman shook her head. "The rooster lives in the pen across the lane. These hens haven't seen him in months." And yet the nest boxes were full, six brown eggs sitting in the straw with no rooster anywhere near.

"So the eggs happen anyway," Gage said, staring into his basket, "but these ones could never be chicks."

"That's kind of amazing," Eliza said. "They look exactly like the other kind. You can't tell by looking."

"Maybe you can't," Lea said. "Maybe it's subjective, whether an egg seems special. But it either has a chick in it or it doesn't."

At the farmhouse kitchen, the cook cracked one of Gage's eggs into a bowl for a demonstration on nineteenth-century baking. The yolk sat round and golden and empty of any beginning. Gage held the basket a little tighter for the rest of the afternoon, and Lea kept glancing at the hens, wondering what else they did without anyone noticing.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
Grace had exactly four dollars and fifty cents in her jacket pocket, and the new SneakFleet sneakers cost way more than that, but she rode the bus home from school anyway, staring at the ad above the window. It showed a crowd of thousands, all wearing the shoes, with giant letters that said "JOIN THE MILLIONS WHO ALREADY SWITCHED." Behind her, Harlow leaned over the seat.

"See?" Harlow said. "Everybody has them. Madelyn got hers Saturday. If we don't get them before the dance, we'll be like the only two people there in regular shoes. They'll practically exclude us from the whole seventh grade."

Grace looked at the ad again. "What do they actually do better? It just says millions of people switched. It doesn't say one thing about the shoes."

Harlow shrugged. "It doesn't have to. That's the point. It's a big crowd."

The bus shudders around a corner and Grace kept thinking. Millions of people could mean anything. If the company sold a shoe to every kid in every school in the country, that would be millions, and it still wouldn't tell her whether the shoe lasted one month or fell apart in the rain. She turned the idea over, testing it. A big number of buyers wasn't a reason. It was just a picture of a crowd.

"They're doing a trick," she said slowly. "It's called a bandwagon appeal. It makes you want to buy because everyone else did, so you feel like you belong, instead of giving you a real reason."

Harlow frowned. "So you're not getting them?"

"I want to belong too," Grace said. "I just don't want to pay ninety dollars for a feeling."

At their stop, Ms. Ramos was waiting to board with her grocery bags, and Grace held the door. "Excuse me, Ms. Ramos," she said. "You're a teacher. If an ad just says join the millions who already switched, and never says what the thing does better, is that a real reason?"

Ms. Ramos smiled. "Sounds like you already answered yourself."

That weekend Grace counted the ads in the magazine at the dentist's office. Eleven of them. Nine used a famous basketball player saying the shoes made him a champion, or words like "revolutionary" and "legendary" that sounded amazing and meant nothing. Only two ads mentioned anything the product actually did, and one of those was a percentage claim about battery life. She copied them both into her notebook.

On Monday she found Harlow at her locker. "I can't afford SneakFleets anyway," Grace said, "so I'm going to prove they're not magic. Madelyn's had hers a week. If they're really revolutionary, they'll still look new by the dance." Madelyn, walking past, held up one foot. The toe was already scuffed gray. Harlow stared at it, then laughed.

"Okay," Harlow said. "New plan. We show up in whatever we've got, and we dance anyway."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker. This is called the fight-or-flight response.
story:
Owen locked the bathroom door and set his hands on the edge of the sink. In the mirror his face was pale, and when he held one hand flat against the counter, it trembled anyway. His heart was slamming like he'd sprinted up three flights of stairs, though all he'd done was walk down the hallway to this bathroom, fifteen minutes before the geography bee was supposed to start. He pressed two fingers under his jaw and counted. Too fast. Way too fast.

He was getting sick. That was the obvious answer. People got the flu in November, and the cafeteria pizza at lunch had been heavy enough that his stomach still hadn't managed to digest it, and now his whole body was quitting on him. He should find Ms. Villanueva and tell her Noemi would have to take his spot on the team. She'd been alternate for a reason, though, and he'd studied the rivers of South America for two weeks. He opened the cabinet to look for something, anything, and found only his mother's prescription for her migraines, label faded, and a box of bandages. Nothing for a racing heart.

There was a knock on the door. "Owen? They're doing name tags." It was Alejandro, who had the locker next to his and never knocked on anything quietly.

"In a minute," Owen called back. His voice came out thin. He turned on the tap and splashed cold water on his face, and standing there dripping, he started to think instead of panic. Sick people got a fever, or a sore throat, or a stuffy nose. He had none of that. What he had was a fast heartbeat, quick shallow breathing, and shaking hands. Exactly like last spring, before the piano recital, when he'd been sure he was coming down with something and had felt completely fine by the next morning.

His mother had said something then, standing in the kitchen with her tea. "When your brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline," she'd said, "and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker." He'd asked what threat, since nobody was chasing him, and she'd shrugged. "It's called the fight-or-flight response. Your body can't tell a recital from a bear." He hadn't really believed her. His body couldn't be that dumb.

But here it was again, the same pattern, and if his mother was right, then he wasn't sick at all, and if he wasn't sick, then maybe he could do something about it. His brain thought the geography bee was a bear. Fine. He couldn't reason with a bear, but he could work the other end, the breathing. Slow breaths in, long breaths out, the way the gym teacher had them do after sprints. He breathed in for four counts and out for six, resting his hands on the cool synthetic marble of the counter so the shaking had something steady under it. He did it again. And again. Slowly, his breathing lengthened, and then, like something settling, his heartbeat came down with it. Not all the way. But enough.

The sleep part he'd have to fix later, because that was the other thing he could see now, looking back over the past week: two nights of flashcards past midnight, one night of staring at the ceiling. No wonder his body had run out of ways to stay calm. He'd trade the studying for sleep next time, maybe, and that felt like a loss too, because the flashcards were why he knew the Amazon had the largest discharge of any river on Earth.

He dried his face, checked the mirror once more, and unlocked the door. Alejandro was leaning against the wall with a marker and a blank name tag. "Thought you fell in."

"Almost," Owen said, and held out his hand for the tag. It was still trembling, just barely, so he took another slow breath, in for four, out for six, right there in the hallway, and followed Alejandro toward the gym.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Nicene Creed, recited in many Christian churches, ends by looking forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.
story:
The funeral was for Romy's great-aunt Ida, and the priest's voice carried over the rows of headstones like a stone skipping water. At the very end he said the congregation looked forward to "the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come," and everyone repeated it, even Romy's mother, even the cousins who hadn't been inside a church in years. Romy mouthed along but didn't say the words. She was too busy noticing them.

Afterward, while the adults clustered around the flower cart, she found Sean sitting on the low stone wall that ran along the cemetery's east fence. His grandfather was buried somewhere in the back rows, under a Star of David, and Sean had told her once that his family said kaddish for the dead, a prayer in Aramaic that never once mentioned dying. "How does your side explain what happens after?" she asked him. "Yours just promised resurrection and a world to come. That's a lot of detail."

Sean shrugged. "Ours doesn't really do detail. You praise God, that's the kaddish. Nobody hands you a map." He picked at a piece of moss on the wall. "Why, does it matter to you?"

Romy had been turning that over all week, ever since her mother mentioned the funeral. Her grandmother was Catholic and her father's family was Jewish, and she had never thought to compare them side by side, like two answers to the same homework question. Her idea, and it felt almost too simple to be plausible, was this: if she could stand in each tradition's holy place and listen for what people actually said about the dead, she could assess the difference for herself instead of guessing. "Come with me Sunday," she said. "My grandmother's church, then your synagogue. Just to listen. We'll test the logic of it."

On Sunday they sat in the back pew of St. Brigid's, and when the congregation stood and recited the creed, Romy heard it again, whole and unmistakable: the Nicene Creed, the one from the funeral, ending with the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. At the synagogue afterward they stood beside Sean's father while he prayed, and Romy listened hard for anything like a promise. There was praise, there was peace, there was God's great name. There was no map, exactly as Sean had said.

Walking home through the cemetery shortcut, past great-aunt Ida's fresh stone, Romy stopped and read the carved dates. Two traditions, two ways of standing at a grave: one looking forward to a world to come, one sanctifying the world that already was. She couldn't see either one from here, and that, she decided, was the interesting part. "Next," she said, pulling her notebook from her backpack, "we find out what the Muslims say."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
The poster on the wall said "Stress" in big letters, but the S had peeled off, so it said "tress," and Maeva kept staring at it because looking at Ms. Van Dijk's door was easier than looking at Fynn. Fynn sat beside her with his elbows on his knees, and he had lost the track meet on Tuesday and then slept through Wednesday's quiz, and today he had asked her to come here, so here she was.

"Sit anywhere," said Ms. Van Dijk, waving at the squishy chairs. "Fynn, you wanted to talk about the last few weeks?"

"I keep being tired," Fynn said. "Like, all the time. Even when I sleep."

Maeva had a theory, and she had spent all of lunch testing it against what she knew. Fynn's dad had been in the hospital for six weeks. Six weeks of worrying before every phone call, before every afternoon. She turned it over like a math problem. If a bad day made you tired, that was one thing. But this was weeks, and weeks was different. She remembered the nurse at the hospital, the one who had stopped to talk to them in the hallway while they waited, and what she'd said.

"Cortisol," Maeva said. "That's the hormone thing. Remember? The nurse said it's made by the adrenal glands and it rises during stress." Fynn nodded slowly. "And she said when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high. Six weeks is a long time."

Ms. Van Dijk leaned forward. "That's what the doctor told your dad's nurse to pass along, isn't it, Fynn? Not a diagnosis, just a reason."

"Yeah." Fynn rubbed his eyes. "She said that's why I feel run down. My anxiety's been running the whole time, like a faucet nobody shut."

"A valve," Maeva said. "And nobody shut the valve." It came out sharper than she meant, and she heard what was underneath it. She was angry. Not at Fynn. At the kids in their group chat who had sent him forty messages about the meet, at the ones who kept asking if his dad was going to be okay, at everyone who kept opening the valve.

"So here's the test," she said. "If weeks of stress keep the cortisol high, then less stress is the thing to try. Coping, the nurse called it. Real coping, not just waiting." She pulled out the notebook she had filled during last period. "I wrote down everything that hits you in a day. The group chat. The hospital calls after nine. Candice asking you to cover her paper route."

"Boundaries," Ms. Van Dijk said. "That's the word for the shut-off part."

Fynn looked at the list. He took the pen out of Maeva's hand and drew a line through the group chat. Then through the paper route. Then through after-nine calls, and he wrote his aunt's number there instead, because she was already at the hospital and didn't need to be told twice.

"One week," he said. "Then we see if I'm still a zombie."

"Seven days," Maeva said. "I'm counting."

Ms. Van Dijk turned the notebook around to face them both and wrote nurture across the top of the page, under the word Monday.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
Megan stood at the edge of her grandmother's backyard with the folded paper in her hand, the same paper she had carried around for two weeks. The reading for her quinceañera Mass was printed on it, and in three weeks she would stand in front of everyone she knew and say it without the paper. At the long table under the string lights, her cousins were arguing about who would donate the flowers for the church, and her aunt was telling someone that the guest list had to be proportional to the size of the hall, half as many chairs as invitations sent.

"You've been staring at that thing since lunch," Haniya said, sliding onto the bench beside her. "My mom says hi, by the way. She couldn't come today."

"I keep losing the middle part," Megan said. "The beginning is fine and the end is fine, but the middle just falls apart every time."

Haniya tapped the paper. "So say it here. Nobody's listening."

Megan started strong, her voice steady through the first lines, and then, exactly where she predicted, the words slid away from her. She stopped, frowned, and started the middle again. It collapsed again at the same word.

"That's weird," Haniya said. "It's the same place every time."

Megan looked at the paper, then at the yard. Her little cousins were running laps around the lemon tree, shouting a counting rhyme. She watched them for a moment. "They remember the rhyme because they move while they say it," she said slowly. "Maybe my brain needs something to hang the middle on." She held up the paper. "I'm going to walk. One lap of the yard for the whole reading, and if I hit the bad spot, I'll mark where my feet are."

She walked the perimeter of the grass, saying the reading out loud, and this time when she reached the middle her feet were passing the rosebush by the fence. She stumbled, stopped, and stood there. On the second lap she slowed her steps as she came to the rosebush, and the words came with her, one line for every two steps, all the way through the part that had been crumbling. She finished the last sentence at the porch steps and turned around, grinning.

Ms. Sharma, the neighbor who had come over for the cake, was watering her side of the hedge and had clearly heard everything. "The Mass of thanksgiving will be lucky to have you," she said. "My reading at my own wedding fell apart until I did it while washing dishes."

"Every day, then," Megan said. "One reading, one walk around the block."

Haniya held out her hand for the paper. "Fold it up. You don't need it anymore."

Megan folded it along its worn creases and put it in her back pocket. "Lap three," she said, and set off past the lemon tree.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: Outlining first separates planning from sentence-writing, so a writer decides what to say before worrying about how to word it.
story:
Gavin had written one sentence in forty minutes, and he had crossed it out twice. The essay prompt sat on the kitchen table in front of him: Is the school's morning news program propaganda, or a fair source of information? He was supposed to state his position in a single thesis sentence, then build a three-point argument before drafting. He kept starting the thesis and getting tangled in the wording, and every time he crossed it out, the blank page seemed larger.

Alaina came in through the back door, dropped her backpack on a chair, and leaned over his paper. "You've been on that since I texted you."

"I can't get the first sentence right," Gavin said. "If the thesis sounds weird, the whole essay is weird."

"So skip the sentence part." She slid a glass of water across the table toward him, and sunlight refracted through it, laying a wobbling stripe of light across his notebook. "Do the plan first. My cousin calls it the bullet-point outline. You write down what you want to say, then worry about how to word it later."

Gavin frowned at her. "Mr. Lewandowski said thesis first."

"He said thesis, outline, then draft. He didn't say you have to word the thesis in perfect sentences right away. Write it ugly."

Gavin turned to a fresh page. Under a heading that just said ARGUMENT, he scrawled three fast bullets: morning news only shows one side of the fundraiser fight; the anchors never interview anyone against it; the principal picks every story himself. No sentences, no punctuation, half of it abbreviations. It took him four minutes.

Then something shifted. Staring at the three bullets instead of a blank page, he could suddenly see the shape of the whole essay, and the thesis came out almost whole: "The morning news program is not an impartial source because it shows only one side, silences opposing voices, and lets one person decide what counts as news." He read it to Alaina.

"That's propaganda, right there," she said, tapping his third bullet. "One guy controlling all the stories. Use that word."

Gavin wrote it in. Behind the glass of water, the stripe of light had crawled up the wall, and his outline was still ugly, and it didn't matter anymore. He flipped to a clean sheet and started the draft.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under first-past-the-post, a candidate with 40 votes beats rivals with 35 and 25 votes, even though 60 of the 100 voters chose someone else.
story:
The community centre had been a polling station all day, and now that the real voters had gone home, Mr. Rao was letting the student volunteers run a mock election with pretend ballots. Leo had drawn the tally sheet himself. He sat at a folding table near the window, sorting ballots into three piles, one per candidate.

"Forty for Red Party," he announced. "Thirty-five for Blue. Twenty-five for Green." Paisley wrote the numbers on the board while Madelyn stacked the ballots so Mr. Rao could classify them again if anyone disputed the count. One hundred ballots, three parties, no argument about the arithmetic.

"Red wins," Paisley said, and circled the forty.

Leo looked at the board. Something about it bothered him, the way a noise you hear every night bothers you only when you finally listen. He counted again, this time adding the two losing piles together. "Wait," he said. "Sixty people picked Blue or Green. Only forty picked Red. Red wins anyway?"

"That's first-past-the-post," Madelyn said. "Most votes takes the seat."

"Most out of the three," Leo said. "Not most out of everybody." He took a fresh sheet and drew a long rectangle divided into three sections, sized to match the numbers: forty percent, thirty-five, twenty-five. "If it worked like this, like the seats match the votes, then Red wouldn't just take everything. Blue and Green would get something too."

"Proportional representation," Paisley read off the sample ballot's back page, where the mock election rules were printed. She had known the whole time, Leo realized. She had circled Red's win without a word just to see if he would notice. "Mr. Rao said to let you find it," she admitted. "He said you'd get there faster if we didn't hand it to you."

Rain started against the window, the first of the monsoon season, loud enough that they had to raise their voices. Mr. Rao came over with the boxed real ballots under one arm, ready to seal them for the night. He glanced at Leo's rectangle and the three piles on the table.

"So," Mr. Rao said. "Same hundred voters, two different results. Which one do you want to present at Monday's assembly?"

Leo tapped the rectangle. "This one. But I'll show them the piles first, and let them count it themselves." He slid the forty Red ballots across the table until they sat apart from the sixty others. "Sixty here, forty there," he said. "Then I'll ask who won."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and old magazines, and Alice sat between Yusuf and an elderly man with a cast on his wrist. Her own arm, wrapped in fresh plaster from the fall off the bleachers, rested in a sling. Yusuf was reading a poster about bone health out loud in an assertive announcer voice, which made the elderly man chuckle.

"Six weeks," the man said, tapping his cast. "That's what they told me. Six weeks in this thing. What did they tell you?"

Alice held up two fingers, then decided that looked like a peace sign, then said, "Three, maybe four. The doctor said probably three." She hadn't thought about it until now. Same building, same kind of break, the man had said, a clean break near the wrist. Yet his number was nearly double hers. Yusuf shrugged when she glanced at him, but the question had already settled into her mind like a stone in a shoe.

She tested her idea the only way she could, by gathering evidence. She asked the man how old his granddaughter was, and he said she'd broken her ankle last summer. "Four weeks in a cast," he said, and then, before Alice could ask, "they told me I'd need longer than her, and they were right. Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break. That's what her doctor said, anyway." He said it like testimony, a hand raised in a courtroom, and Yusuf laughed so hard the receptionist looked over. Alice wrote the words on the fogged window with her good hand, watching them condense into little droplets and run.

"Wait," she said slowly, working it through. "So it's not about how careful you are, or how bad the break looks. It's just... age. You heal slower because you're older, and I heal faster because I'm fourteen." The man nodded, looking a little rueful about it. "Faster isn't always better, though," he said. "My granddaughter was back on the soccer field in a month and a half, and she re-injured the same ankle by October. You'll be out of that cast before the season even starts." Alice thought of the gymnastics meet she'd missed, the one where Isabella had taken her spot on bars and scored higher than Alice ever had. Fast-healing bones wouldn't fix that.

When the nurse called her name, Alice stood up, and the man raised his good hand in a small salute. "Four weeks, tops," she said to Yusuf, and walked through the door.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
The reading was eleven lines long, and Hayden had to recite it from memory at his grandmother's house on Saturday, in front of the whole family. He had been mouthing the words for two days and kept losing them around line six. On Thursday he rode his bike to his grandfather's place, a dilapidated yellow house at the end of Fell Street, and spread the paper on the kitchen table.

"The words won't stick," he told his grandfather. "I say them and they slide right off."

His grandfather was watering a fern by the window. "When I was your age, I put each line in a room of this house," he said. "Line one at the front door. Line two on the stairs. When my turn came, I walked the whole route in my head and the lines came with it."

Hayden frowned. "You walked the house in your mind?"

"That's the method of loci," his grandfather said. "You link each part of the text to a place along a route you know, then walk that route to recall it."

Hayden tried it. He taped the paper inside the front door and read line one there until the words and the peeling paint belonged together in his head. Line two went on the third stair, where the carpet was worn pale. Line three sat on the kitchen table next to the thermostat, which his grandfather kept at seventy because he claimed the furnace could not accelerate fast enough on cold mornings. By the time Hayden placed line six on the bathroom sink, he noticed something: the rooms were doing the remembering for him. He only had to picture the hallway and the words arrived, attached to each doorway like coats on hooks.

On Saturday the living room filled with aunts and cousins, and Mikaela from his class slipped in at the back because he had invited her. She caught his eye and tapped her temple twice. When his name was called, Hayden closed his eyes, stepped onto the front porch in his mind, and started walking. Door, stair, table, sink. The lines came out in order, all eleven, and he opened his eyes on the last word to see his grandfather nodding once, quickly, the way he did.

Afterward Mikaela found him by the food table. "Teach me that," she said. "I have fifty vocabulary words for Monday."

"Fine," Hayden said. "But you have to walk me through your house first."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Jack stood at the edge of the school parking lot, holding the corsage box so tightly that the ribbon bit into his thumb. The gym doors glowed yellow at the far end of the lot, and music thumped through them like a second heartbeat. He had been standing there for eleven minutes. He knew because he was counting, which was the problem, because counting was all he ever did instead of moving.

Ayaan found him first, leaning against a light pole with his tie already loosened. "You're boycotting the dance from out here?" he asked. "That's not how boycotting works. You have to actually not go in."

"I'm going in," Jack said. "I'm waiting for Gracelyn."

Gracelyn was waiting too, on the other side of the lot, near the monsoon of noise pouring from a science classroom where the AV club was testing speakers. She had told Jack at lunch that she wasn't sure about the dancing part. Jack had made the mistake of saying, "You don't have to dance," which was the same thing as saying don't, and she had gone quiet on him. He'd replayed that moment all week, weighing whether he should have said something else, or nothing at all. He still didn't know.

He crossed the lot to her, and she held up her phone before he could apologize. "Look at this," she said. On the screen, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing and stepping to a pop song, perfectly in time. "Snowball," Gracelyn said. "Ayaan found the video. He's notorious for it."

"He's a bird," Jack said. "Birds can't dance."

"He can. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball could move in time to music." She swiped to a second clip. "Watch. When they change the tempo, he adjusts."

Jack watched the bird slow down and speed up with the beat, crest bouncing, and something in his chest untangled a little. If a cockatoo could find the rhythm and follow it when it changed, then the rhythm was real, out there, something you could find and hold onto. It wasn't a talent you were born with or without. It was a rule you could test.

"So here's my theory," he said, keeping his voice steady. "You don't have to be good. You just have to find the beat and match it. If Snowball can adjust when the tempo changes, we can adjust when the song changes."

Gracelyn looked at the gym doors, then at the corsage box, then at him. "That's your big idea? Be like a parrot?"

"Be like a scientist's parrot."

She laughed, and the laugh decided more than either of them said out loud, because the thing she'd actually been waiting for all week was a sign that Jack would meet her halfway instead of managing her. She took his arm and they walked across the lot together, Ayaan falling in behind them like a bodyguard.

Inside, the floor was packed and the music was terrible and wonderful. Jack found the beat with his foot, counting, and then stopped counting and just moved. When the DJ changed the tempo mid-song, Gracelyn caught his eye and slowed with it, matching him step for step, and Jack realized she had been able to dance the whole time.

"You waited outside because of me, didn't you," he said over the music. "Not because you were scared."

Gracelyn kept dancing. "Figure it out, Patel."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
story:
Harrison had been standing by the climbing bars for ten minutes before he noticed the pattern. Randy was teasing Eesa about his accent, the way he said "thirty" like "tirty," and after every joke Randy's eyes flicked sideways, quick as a clock hand, toward the three boys laughing beside the slide. Harrison was one of them. He had laughed too, just a small snort, because it seemed safer than standing there with a flat face.

"Say it again," Randy said. "Tirty. Come on, it's great." Eesa's shoulders had drawn up around his ears, but he smiled a little, the way you do when you hope smiling will end something.

Harrison thought about the flicking eyes. If Randy kept checking the laughing group, maybe the laughing was the fuel, the way a generator needs gas before it will run at all. Take away the fuel and the machine ought to sputter out. He could presume that, at least. It was a small idea, easy to test. The next joke came, something about Eesa ordering "tirty tacos," and Harrison let his mouth stay closed. He looked at the ground, then up at the sky, like a kid checking the weather.

Randy told another one anyway. But this time the glance toward the group was longer, and when the laughter came back thinner, one boy distracted by a phone, Randy's voice lost a little of its bounce. The jokes had been getting the group's approval, and Harrison had been part of that without ever deciding to be. Laughing to fit in was its own kind of signal, like waving a green flag he hadn't meant to wave.

"Hey, Randy," Harrison said, walking over. He kept his voice easy, hands in his pockets. "Eesa's got that new deck of cards in his bag. The ones from Istanbul. You want to see them or what?"

Randy blinked. Jokes needed an audience, and now Harrison was offering a different show entirely. "I guess," he said.

Eesa unzipped his bag slowly, watching Harrison out of the corner of his eye, and spread the cards on the bench. The backs were painted with vines and gold birds, delicate work, nothing like the plain decks everyone else had. Even the kid with the phone drifted over. Randy picked up a card and turned it over twice, as if the picture might change.

"They had them at this shop near my grandmother's," Eesa said. His shoulders had come down from his ears.

"Deal us in," Harrison said, and sat down on the bench between his two classmates, the cards flashing gold in the afternoon light.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
The potato salad was nearly gone when Lucas cornered his cousin by the porch railing. "Okay, one question. Who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775?" Amara shrugged. Jonah, mouth full of chips, said, "The British. Obviously."

"It's not obvious," Lucas said. He pulled out the two photocopies Ms. Foster had given the history club before summer break. "I've been reading these all week." Last Tuesday at the library, he'd set the pages side by side, expecting one to fall apart. Instead, both sounded completely sure.

"Read this one," he said, handing Amara the first sheet. "That's a colonial witness. He says the British fired first." He gave her the second. "That's a British witness. He says the colonists fired first." Amara read, frowning. "So somebody's lying."

"That's what I thought too," Lucas said. He glanced toward the picnic table, where Ms. Foster, his neighbor, was balancing a paper plate. She'd been drafted into the party because she was the only adult who would talk about history longer than his uncle would talk about his lawn. She raised an eyebrow at him but said nothing.

Here was Lucas's test, the one he'd been building toward. "What if nobody's lying?" he said. "What if both sides believed it was the other guy?" He thought of the smoke, the noise, a hundred frightened men on each side of a green at dawn. His idea was simple: memory fills in whatever fits what you already fear. "Think about the probability," he went on. "Two armies facing each other, everyone jumpy, a shot rings out in the confusion. Nobody can prove who violated the peace first, because every witness saw it from behind their own line."

Jonah swallowed his chips. "So we'll never know?"

"Historians still don't know," Ms. Foster said, finally setting down her plate. "That's the honest answer."

Jonah, who had announced at the start of the summer that history was just dates, looked at the two pages again. "So the truth just... got lost?" Lucas nodded. For a second nobody spoke. Then Jonah said, "I changed my mind, by the way. History isn't boring. It's a mystery nobody solved." He grabbed another handful of chips. "Still not doing your club poster, though. I'm negligent about posters. It's my whole style."

Lucas laughed. From the yard, his uncle yelled that the sparklers were lit, and the three of them ran for the grass before the flames burned out.
